title: Trump’s Iran Deal: A Fragile Pause in a Devastating War
summary: After three and a half months of war that has killed thousands, destabilized the Middle East, and pushed millions into poverty, a glimmer of hope emerged this week. On Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed a memorandum of understanding aimed at ending military operations and launching broader negotiations. The preliminary agreement immediately lifted the U.S. naval blockade on Iran and promised to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil passes. “Ships of the World, start your engines. Let the oil flow!” Trump celebrated on Truth Social. But the deal is extraordinarily fragile. It creates a 60-day window — extendable only by mutual consent — to resolve decades of enmity. Trump himself underscored its tenuous nature at the G7 summit in France: “If I don’t like it, if they don’t behave, we’ll go right back to dropping bombs right smack in the middle of their head.” The biggest immediate test is Lebanon. The memorandum promises to end all military operations, including there, where Israel has been waging a major offensive against the Iranian-backed militia Hezbollah. Yet hours after the signing, Israeli airstrikes killed at least 18 people in Lebanon, and Israel reported four of its own soldiers dead in southern Lebanon. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi insisted that without a full Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory, “the war has not fully come to an end.” Israel was not a party to the negotiations. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has remained defiant, saying his troops will stay as long as necessary for Israel’s security. Far-right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir declared, “Trump’s agreement does not bind us.” The rift between Trump and Netanyahu has become extraordinarily open. Vice President JD Vance, who delayed a trip to Switzerland for further talks, warned Israeli critics that “Donald J. Trump is the only head of state in the entire world who is sympathetic to the nation of Israel at this moment in time.” With thousands already dead and a global economy rattled, the world now watches to see if this fragile paper can hold — or if the bombs will start falling again.
why_it_matters: If this deal collapses, a wider Middle Eastern war could once again send oil prices soaring, upending everything from family travel costs to the global economy that will shape your future job market.

background_read: The deep distrust between the United States and Iran goes back to the 1979 Iranian Revolution, when American hostages were held for 444 days, and has been fueled by decades of disputes over Iran's nuclear program.

In 2015, Iran signed a deal with world powers to limit its nuclear activities in exchange for relief from punishing sanctions, but President Trump pulled the U.S. out of that deal in 2018, saying it was too weak.

The Strait of Hormuz (the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which a fifth of the world's oil is shipped) has been a flashpoint before: Iran has threatened to block it, and the U.S. Navy has patrolled it to keep oil flowing, making any blockade a major global economic danger.

The G7 summit (the annual meeting of leaders from seven of the world's largest advanced economies: Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States) often sees Trump making dramatic statements, as he did here.

Hezbollah (a powerful Shia Muslim political and military group in Lebanon, backed by Iran) has been a key part of Iran's influence in the Middle East, and earlier clashes between Israel and Hezbollah have often risked turning into full-scale regional war.

perspectives.description: The memorandum shows that even after brutal conflict, leaders can choose talks over bombs. Lifting the blockade immediately eases suffering for ordinary Iranians and helps stabilize world oil markets, which benefits everyone.

The deal is so thin that it could be shattered by a single airstrike. Israel was not even at the table, and its leaders see the agreement as an American move that does not guarantee their security, meaning the violence could quickly resume and drag the region even deeper into war.

The U.S.-Iran relationship has been defined by short-lived diplomatic moments often followed by renewed hostility. Even if this pause holds for 60 days, decades of mutual suspicion — from the hostage crisis to the nuclear program — mean that lasting trust is almost impossible to build in a single agreement.

The world is watching to see whether the 60-day window can become true negotiations, perhaps pulling in Israel and Iran's other rivals. If it fails, the cycle of bombing and blockade will not only kill more people but could permanently reshape energy supply routes and alliances, with fallout for your generation.
